summary: This unit teaches you to prepare an operational (operating) budget for a department or small business: link it to plans, choose a budgeting method, gather data and write assumptions, split costs into fixed and variable, calculate income and cost lines, phase the budget by month, build it in a spreadsheet, check and test it, get it approved, revise it, and set it up for monitoring against actual results.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. An **operational budget** (also called an operating budget) is a plan of expected income and running costs for a period, usually twelve months. Managers of departments, hotels, schools, agencies and small firms prepare one each year, and use it afterwards to control spending and judge performance.

At Level 5 you prepare the budget, not only read one. You must be able to turn plans into figures, justify the figures, build them in a spreadsheet, defend the draft to senior management, and hand over a budget that others can monitor.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Understand what the budget is for
Explain operating and capital budgets, link the budget to the organisation's goals and follow a timetable.
Compare incremental, zero-based, fixed, flexible and rolling budgets and choose the one that suits the situation.
Use last year's actuals, adjust for known changes, and write down the assumptions the figures rest on.
Work out income, fixed, variable and staff costs, include a contingency, and add up correctly.
Spread the yearly figures over the months in which they fall, in a clear layout, normally in a spreadsheet.
Check the figures twice, test the key assumptions, and consult those who know the work.
Present the draft, respond to requests for cuts by priority, and communicate the approved budget.
Name budget holders, report variances and use flexible budgets to compare fairly.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions and calculations (cost behaviour, phasing, price rises, percentage cuts, variances).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as zero-based, contingency, limiting factor, master budget) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done in a group: a draft twelve-month operating budget in a spreadsheet from a data pack, and a revised budget that meets a cut of 8%, with a flexible budget table and a presentation.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, by two different routes. A budget that is wrong by a factor of ten (J$1,950,000 or J$19,500,000?) is a common slip: check that the answer is sensible.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The purpose of budgets and the budgeting timetable

ul: **Planning**: turns goals into money and resources.
**Co-ordination**: makes departments work to one plan.
**Control**: gives a standard to compare actual results with.
**Responsibility**: gives each manager a named part of the plan.
**Communication and motivation**: tells people the targets and limits.

head: Budget
What it covers
Example
rows: Expected income and running costs for the period
A new air-conditioning plant, a van, machinery, a building
When cash comes in and goes out, month by month
Credit sales received after 30 days; loan payments
The overall budget that brings together all the departmental and functional budgets
The firm's income, costs, cash and assets in one plan

blocks.p: The cash budget is prepared **from** the operating budget, because the operating budget shows what will be earned and spent, and the cash budget shows **when** the money moves. A cash budget does not replace the operating budget.

A budget must be based first on **the organisation's goals and plans for the year**, such as opening a new service, training staff or serving more customers. Do not start from the amount you would like to spend, from what other departments are spending, or from last year's figures with a flat percentage added. These may be used later as checks, but they are not the starting point.

A timetable says who does what and by when, so every stage is finished in time for approval: guidelines issued, data gathered, drafts prepared, consultation, review, approval, communication. Without one, the review stage gets skipped when time runs out.

flow: Finance issues the guidelines, templates and the planning assumptions
Departments gather data and draft their budgets
Managers consult team leaders and check the drafts
Drafts are reviewed and combined into the master budget
Senior management or the board approves the budget
Approved budgets are communicated to budget holders

blocks.note: In the public sector, the budget calendar is set by the ministry of finance or the parent ministry, and funds are voted for the financial year. In Jamaica the financial year for government runs from 1 April to 31 March. Private firms may use a different year.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Method
How it works
Strength
Weakness
Best when
rows: Start from last year's budget or actuals and adjust for known changes
Carries forward waste and old costs without question
Activity changes little from year to year
Start from zero each year; every cost line must be justified
Removes out-of-date costs; focuses on value
Costs have grown for years without review; a new or restructured department
One budget set for a single planned level of activity
Unfair comparison if activity differs from plan
Cost allowances change with the actual level of activity
Fair comparison at any activity level
Needs costs split into fixed and variable
Activity varies, as in hotels, kitchens, call centres
Updated each period (month or quarter), adding a new period at the end so there is always a full period ahead
Always up to date; reflects change
Costs are budgeted from the activities that cause them

blocks.p: **Incremental** budgeting means starting from last year's budget and adjusting it. **Zero-based** means starting from zero and justifying every cost line. If managers at a hotel suspect that old costs are carried forward without question, zero-based budgeting helps most; it should be done thoroughly at least every few years, with incremental budgeting in between.

blocks.note: Do not confuse a fixed budget (set once for one activity level) with fixed costs (costs that do not change with output in the short term).
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Gathering data, assumptions and cost behaviour

ul: **Last year's actual costs**, by month, adjusted for changes: the most reliable starting point.
This year's figures to date.
Known changes: new services, staffing, contracts, price rises, wage settlements, new equipment, closures.
Planned activity: number of customers, rooms sold, students, calls, jobs.
Quotations and price lists from suppliers (current prices, not brochures from a different time).
Policies and limits from senior management.

blocks.p: Do not use a guess by the newest member of staff, or figures from a firm in a different industry.

Every budget is a forecast, so it rests on **assumptions**: the level of activity, prices, wage rates, inflation, the exchange rate, staffing, the timing of new services and customers' payment habits. Write down the key assumptions, with their source, on a separate sheet, so reviewers can see and test what the figures rest on. If an assumption is wrong, every figure that depends on it will be wrong too.

ul: **Price rises**: if supplies cost J$2,500,000 this year and prices are expected to rise by 6% for the same volume, next year's budget is J$2,500,000 x 1.06 = J$2,650,000.

**Foreign currency**: if you buy supplies priced in US dollars, state the exchange rate assumed (for example J$155 to US$1), and test what happens if the J$ weakens. Do not leave the exchange rate out or use an old one.
**Volume**: say what activity level the budget assumes, such as 3,000 meals a month.

head: Cost type
Behaviour
Examples
rows: Stays the same in total in the short term whatever the output
Monthly rent, insurance on the building, a manager's monthly salary
Changes in total in direct line with output
Raw materials, ingredients, packaging, sales commission
An electricity bill with a fixed monthly charge plus a charge per kilowatt-hour; a phone plan with line rental plus call charges
Fixed until output passes a level, then jumps
A new supervisor needed for every 20 staff

blocks.p: Total cost = fixed costs + (variable cost per unit x number of units). If fixed costs are J$400,000 a month and variable cost is J$250 a unit, the budget for 2,000 units is J$400,000 + (J$250 x 2,000) = J$400,000 + J$500,000 = J$900,000. If each meal costs J$650 in ingredients and 3,000 meals are planned, the ingredient budget is J$650 x 3,000 = J$1,950,000.

blocks.h: Limiting factor and the order of preparation

blocks.p: A **limiting factor** (or principal budget factor) is the one resource that limits how much a firm can do: sales demand, machine time, skilled staff, space. Build the budget around it. If a firm could sell 10,000 units but has machine time for only 7,000, the budget is built around 7,000 units. Do not use the manager's hoped-for target of 12,000.
Usually the **sales (income) budget is prepared first**, because production, purchases, staffing and cash all depend on it. If another factor limits output, start with that.

blocks.note: A wish is not a forecast. If you want to plan for higher sales, say what will cause them, such as a new contract or more rooms, and put the evidence in your working papers.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Building the budget: income, costs, staff, phasing and contingency

blocks.p: Income = expected volume x price. A training firm expecting 240 trainees at J$45,000 each budgets J$45,000 x 240 = J$10,800,000. A café selling 1,200 lunches a month at J$900 budgets J$900 x 1,200 = J$1,080,000 a month. Show **GCT at the current rate** separately where it applies, since it is collected for the government and is not income.

ul: Work out each line from its drivers: quantity x price, number of staff x cost per person, number of months x monthly charge.
Split each line into **fixed and variable**.
Use quotations and contracts where you have them.

blocks.p: Budget for more than basic salaries: **employer's statutory contributions** (such as NIS, NHT, education tax and HEART/NSTA Trust contributions, at the rates in force), **overtime, allowances, bonuses, leave and training**. Check what the finance office or human resources department gives you for the cost per person. Example: 6 staff, each costing J$180,000 a month in total, give a staff budget of 6 x J$180,000 x 12 = J$12,960,000 (check: 6 x 180,000 = 1,080,000 a month; x 12 = 12,960,000).
To **phase** a budget is to spread the yearly figures over the months in which they will occur. Phasing shows whether a quiet month is normal or a warning sign, and it makes the cash budget right.

head: Line
How to phase
rows: By the pattern of past years: higher in peak months, lower in the rest
Equally by month (J$2,400,000 a year is J$200,000 a month)
In line with the phased activity
In the month paid; the operating budget may spread them equally, the cash budget shows when paid
By month, including the months with extra pay (such as a bonus)

blocks.p: Example: a guest house expects room income of J$12,000,000 a year, with 65% earned in the five peak months (December to April). Peak: J$12,000,000 x 65% = J$7,800,000, which is J$1,560,000 a month. The other seven months share the remaining 35%, J$4,200,000, which is J$600,000 a month. Check: 5 x 1,560,000 = 7,800,000; 7 x 600,000 = 4,200,000; total J$12,000,000.

A **contingency** is a small amount added to cover likely but uncertain extra costs. It should be based on evidence and clearly labelled, and it should be modest and approved. It is not a fund for gifts to clients, a way to hide profit, or a reason to skip careful estimating. Adding 20% to every line 'just in case' is not honest budgeting: it ties up funds and hides the true need.
If activity rose to 3,000 jobs, a flexible budget gives costs of 3,000 x J$220 = J$660,000 plus J$450,000 = J$1,110,000, income of 3,000 x J$480 = J$1,440,000, and profit of J$330,000.

blocks.note: Rounding: keep exact figures in the workings and round only for display. Show the same unit throughout (J$, not a mix of J$ and J$000).
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Cash budgets, spreadsheets, checking and testing

blocks.h: From the operating budget to the cash budget

blocks.p: A sale in May on 30-day credit terms is recorded as income in May but the cash usually arrives in **June**. A supplier paid after 60 days affects cash two months later. The cash budget turns the operating budget into the money actually received and paid, month by month, so managers can see when an overdraft or surplus will occur.

blocks.h: Building the budget in a spreadsheet

ul: Use separate sheets: **assumptions and inputs**, **workings**, and a **summary**.
Put every input (volumes, prices, rates, exchange rate) in a labelled cell with its source. Use formulas that refer to those cells; never type numbers into formulas.
Changing an input then updates every total at once; that is the main advantage.
Use consistent layout: a line for each income and cost, columns for each month, totals for the year.
Protect formulas and keep a version number and date.
Check **sum ranges include every row**: if a total looks too low, check first that the formulas include all rows, not the fonts or colours.

blocks.p: Layout best suited to managers reading a draft: a line for each income and cost, by month, with totals. Do not give one long paragraph of figures, a copy of every invoice, or one pie chart of the whole year's costs.

flow: Check each calculation twice, by a different route
Check totals, sub-totals and the link between sheets
Compare with last year's actual figures and ask why any line differs a lot
Have a second person check it
Keep working papers for every line

blocks.p: **Working papers** (the calculations, quotations and sources behind each line) let others trace and explain the figures later. They are not there to show other firms how the budget was built or to look thick.

**Sensitivity analysis** asks 'what if?' for key assumptions: what if sales are 10% lower, the exchange rate moves 5%, or prices rise 8% instead of 6%? Change one input and show the effect on profit or cost. It tells managers which assumptions matter most and how much room there is for error.

Consult team leaders. They know the work, the equipment, the waste and the real prices, and they gain a sense of ownership of the budget. They do not give final approval, and consultation is not a way to share blame if the budget fails. The manager must still decide, using the organisation's guidelines.

sections.title: Approval, revision, communication and the public sector

blocks.p: The **board or senior management** usually gives final approval to an operating budget. Present the draft with its assumptions, a short summary of changes from last year, the key risks and the sensitivity results.

Senior management may ask for cuts. Do not cut every line by the same percentage without thought, refuse because the work was careful, or cut the training or safety line to zero. A good response is to **review lines by priority**, protect essential services, identify savings, show the effect of each cut on service, staff and risk, and offer a choice.

A budget only works if the people who spend the money and earn the income understand it. Share it with **budget holders** and explain the targets, limits, reporting dates and who to ask. Do not file it away until next year, post it publicly, or change it weekly without telling people.

In a ministry, agency or municipal corporation, the budget is driven by the services to be provided and by the funds voted or allocated, rather than by sales and profit. The key principles are that **spending must stay within approved amounts and rules**, funds may not be moved between lines except as the rules allow, unspent money is not a bonus for staff, and records must be open to the auditors. Procurement rules apply to purchases.

head: Private firm
Ministry, agency or municipal corporation
rows: Driven by sales and profit targets
Driven by services and the funds allocated
Managers have some freedom to move funds with approval
Strict rules on moving funds between lines
Parliament, the parent ministry or the council approves
Service delivery, value for money and compliance measure success

sections.title: Setting up monitoring: budget holders, variances and flexible budgets

blocks.p: Each budget line should have a **named budget holder**, the manager responsible for watching and explaining it. Without a name, nobody is accountable. The budget holder receives a monthly report comparing actual with budget.
A **variance** is the difference between actual and budget. It is **favourable** if it improves profit (income higher or costs lower than budget) and **adverse** if it reduces profit.

ul: Budgeted J$480,000, actual J$516,000: variance J$36,000 **adverse** (7.5% over).
Labour budgeted J$300,000, actual J$330,000: J$30,000 adverse (10%).
Sales budgeted J$900,000, actual J$950,000: J$50,000 favourable.

blocks.p: If actual activity differs from plan, comparing actual costs with the original budget is unfair. A **flexed budget** restates the budget for the actual activity. Example: variable cost of J$800 per unit plus fixed cost of J$500,000; actual output 1,800 units. Flexed allowance = 800 x 1,800 + 500,000 = 1,440,000 + 500,000 = J$1,940,000. Compare actual cost with that.

Link money to activity with a measure such as **cost per occupied room** for a hotel's housekeeping budget, or **staff hours needed** to handle a planned 50,000 calls in a call centre. Plan these non-financial figures with the money.

blocks.note: Say what the variance means, not only how big it is: timing, price, volume or a one-off cause.
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Operating (operational) budget
A plan of expected income and running costs for a period.
Capital expenditure
Spending on long-lasting assets such as buildings and machinery.
Master budget
The overall budget that brings together all the departmental and functional budgets.
Incremental budgeting
Starting from last year's budget and adjusting it.
Zero-based budgeting
Starting from zero and justifying every cost line.
Flexible budget
A budget whose cost allowances change with the actual level of activity.
Rolling budget
A budget updated each period, always looking a full period ahead.
Fixed cost
A cost that stays the same in total, in the short term, whatever the output.
Variable cost
A cost that changes in total in direct line with output.
Semi-variable cost
A cost with a fixed part and a variable part.
Limiting factor
The one resource that limits how much a firm can produce or sell.
Phasing
Spreading the yearly figures over the months in which they will occur.
Contingency
A small amount added for likely but uncertain extra costs.
Sensitivity analysis
Testing how the result changes if key figures differ from the estimate.
Budget holder
The manager responsible for a budget line or cost centre.
Variance
The difference between actual and budget; favourable if profit improves, adverse if it falls.
Financial year
The twelve-month period that a budget covers.

c1.title: A Montego Bay print shop's monthly budget
c1.text: Sandra Clarke manages a print shop in Montego Bay. She plans 2,500 jobs a month, with an average price of J$480 per job. Paper, ink and plates cost J$220 per job. Fixed costs (rent, salaries and insurance) are J$450,000 a month. A large customer may increase her volume to 3,000 jobs a month.

c2.title: The science department's budget at a secondary school
c2.text: Mr Hugh Palmer, head of science at a Clarendon high school, must prepare next year's budget. Laboratory consumables (chemicals, glassware, specimens) cost J$1,250,000 this year. The principal says prices will rise by about 8%, and the department expects to teach about 5% more students, so it will use about 5% more consumables. Old laboratory items are still being bought each year even though some experiments are no longer taught.

c3.title: Phasing at a Treasure Beach guest house
c3.text: A guest house in Treasure Beach expects room income of J$12,000,000 next year, of which 65% will be earned in the five peak months from December to April. Rent is J$2,400,000 a year. The owner, Marcia Gordon, also takes corporate bookings of J$900,000 in September, which are paid 60 days after the stay.

c4.title: A municipal corporation's markets department
c4.text: The markets and parks department of a municipal corporation in Jamaica has a draft operating budget of J$8,500,000. The council's finance committee asks all departments to cut 6% to meet a shortfall in the corporation's income. The department has a budget holder for each cost line.

c5.title: A security firm's staff costs
c5.text: A Kingston security company employs 14 guards, each costing J$95,000 a month in total (salary and employer contributions). It budgets overtime at 160 hours a month at J$900 an hour. Actual overtime for the year was J$1,980,000. The finance clerk, Mr Peter Dunn, has built the budget in a spreadsheet.

questions.q: What is Sandra's total cost budget for a month at 2,500 jobs?
questions.why: Variable cost = 2,500 x J$220 = J$550,000. Add fixed costs of J$450,000 to get J$1,000,000. Check: cost per job = J$400, and 400 x 2,500 = 1,000,000.

questions.q: What is her budgeted monthly profit at 2,500 jobs?
questions.why: Income = 2,500 x J$480 = J$1,200,000. Costs = J$1,000,000. Profit = J$200,000. Check: profit per job J$80 x 2,500 = J$200,000.

questions.q: If volume rises to 3,000 jobs, what total cost should a flexible budget allow?
questions.why: Only variable cost changes: 3,000 x J$220 = J$660,000, plus fixed J$450,000 = J$1,110,000. Using J$1,000,000 (the old budget) would ignore the extra activity.

questions.q: Which of these costs will rise if the shop prints 3,000 jobs instead of 2,500?
questions.why: Paper and ink vary with the number of jobs. Rent, insurance and a fixed salary stay the same in the short term.

questions.q: Mr Palmer suspects that old items are being bought each year without question. Which method will best deal with this?
o: Incremental budgeting, adding a flat percentage to every line
A fixed budget, copying last year's figures exactly
A rolling budget, adding one month onto last year's plan
Zero-based budgeting, with each item justified from scratch
questions.why: Zero-based budgeting makes every cost line earn its place, so out-of-date items show up. Incremental and copied budgets carry old costs forward.

questions.q: Next year's laboratory consumables budget must allow for both the price rise and the extra use. What figure is correct?
questions.why: Price: 1,250,000 x 1.08 = 1,350,000. Volume: 1,350,000 x 1.05 = 1,417,500. Check the other way round: 1,250,000 x 1.05 = 1,312,500; x 1.08 = 1,417,500. J$1,350,000 allows for price only and J$1,312,500 for extra use only.

questions.q: How should Mr Palmer treat the 8% price rise in his budget?
o: Include it in the figures without mention, so the budget looks more firm
Record it as a stated assumption, with its source, for testing
Leave it out, because the principal's view is not yet a proven fact
Add it to every line in the budget, including those that are not supplies
questions.why: Assumptions must be written down with their source so reviewers can check and test them. Applying it to every line would be wrong, and leaving it out would understate the cost.

questions.q: Why should Mr Palmer talk to his teachers and the laboratory technician before finalising the budget?
o: They know the real needs, waste and prices, and gain ownership
They will give the final approval of the budget on behalf of the board
He can share the blame with them if the budget proves wrong
It will make the budget process longer, and so more thorough
questions.why: Staff know the work and supply detail the manager may miss. Approval rests with senior management, and consultation is for better figures and ownership, not blame.

questions.q: What is the guest house's room income for each of the five peak months?
questions.why: 65% of J$12,000,000 = J$7,800,000 for the five peak months; 7,800,000 / 5 = J$1,560,000. J$7,800,000 is the five-month total.

questions.q: What is the room income for each of the other seven months?
How should the J$2,400,000 rent be phased in the operating budget?
o: Higher in peak months, in line with income
Entirely in December, when the room income is high
Only in the seven months of lower income
questions.why: Rent is a fixed cost that does not depend on activity, so it is spread equally. Matching it to income would be wrong.

questions.q: The J$900,000 corporate booking is for September and is paid 60 days after the stay. In which month does it appear in the cash budget?
questions.why: The income belongs to September in the operating budget, but cash arrives about 60 days later, in November.

questions.q: The finance committee asks every department to cut its draft by 6%. What is the new total for the markets department?
Which approach to the cut is best?
o: Take exactly 6% off every line without any further discussion of priorities
Cut the staff training and safety maintenance lines to zero
Refuse to make any cut at all because the draft was carefully prepared
Review lines by priority, protect essential services and show each effect
questions.why: Priority-based cuts protect services and let decision-makers see the trade-offs. Equal cuts ignore priorities, and cutting safety is unsafe. Refusing may be right only if the cut breaks the law or endangers people.

questions.q: Which principle must the corporation follow in managing the approved budget?
o: Spending must stay within approved amounts, rules and audit
Funds may be moved between any lines whenever the manager decides to
Money left unspent at the year end can be shared among the staff as a bonus
The budget can be kept back from the auditors until after the year end
questions.why: Public-sector budgets are controlled: approved amounts, rules on moving funds and openness to audit. Unspent money is not a bonus.

questions.q: The budget is approved. What should the department head do next?
o: File the budget until the year-end review of the actual results
Send it to the local newspaper to print as a public notice for residents
Meet the budget holders, explain the targets, set reporting dates
Change each line every week and tell the staff about the changes afterwards
questions.why: A budget only works if the people who spend the money understand it. Name the budget holders, explain the targets and set up monthly reports.

questions.q: What is the annual staff cost budget for the 14 guards?
What is the overtime budget for the year?
Actual overtime was J$1,980,000. What is the variance?
o: J$252,000 adverse, which is 14.6% over budget
J$252,000 favourable, which is 14.6% under budget
J$252,000 adverse, which is 12.7% over budget
J$3,708,000 adverse, which is 215% over budget
questions.why: 1,980,000 - 1,728,000 = J$252,000 adverse (more cost than budgeted). 252,000 / 1,728,000 = 14.6% of the budget. 12.7% would divide by the actual figure.

questions.q: The spreadsheet's total staff cost looks too low. What should Mr Dunn check first?
o: The font and colours used on the summary sheet for the board
The file name and the folder where the file was last saved
That the total formula includes every row of the table
The page margins and paper size for printing
questions.why: A low total often means a row is left out of a sum or a number was typed over a formula. Presentation matters later, after the figures are right.
